The transfer is an exact model of representative pairsState meaning and collision-free encodingUse zero-based rows  $0,\dots,5$ . The labels are
$$0=B,\qquad 1=T,\qquad 2=P=V(M).$$
After a column, the retained state is
$$s=(\ell,o,L,R,\phi),$$
with the following meanings:ComponentMeaning $\ell$ The six current labels $o$ Occupancy  $T\cup V(M)$  in the preceding column $L$ Matching edges entering the current column $R$ Matching edges leaving the current column $\phi$ The two accumulated seam-crossing flagsThe source’s key and unpack functions implement
$$k=\operatorname{code}(\ell)+2^{10}o+2^{16}L+2^{22}R+2^{28}\phi.$$
The fields do not overlap. The ternary label code is at most  $728<2^{10}$ ; each mask has six bits; the flag has two bits. Thus the encoding has no collisions on the intended domain.The separately stored base_one mask need not be part of the key: it is determined by  $\ell$  and  $o$ . This matters because the dynamic program merges histories with the same key.Matching degree and vertical completionThe source function vertical checks that:Every bit of  $L$  and  $R$  lies at a  $P$ -vertex. $L\cap R=\varnothing$ .Every remaining  $P$ -vertex is covered by a vertical matching edge.The third condition is implemented by scanning the remaining rows from top to bottom and pairing each first remaining vertex with the next row.That greedy step is exact. The induced graph on the remaining  $P$ -vertices is a disjoint union of consecutive row paths. A path has a perfect matching precisely when its number of vertices is even, and that perfect matching is unique: its first vertex must be matched to its second, after which the same argument applies recursively.Consequently, the code neither overlooks an alternative vertical completion nor introduces an arbitrary choice. Every  $P$ -vertex gets matching degree exactly one.It also correctly permits extra graph adjacencies between matching endpoints. The definition requires  $M$  to be a matching; it does not require an induced matching.Horizontal matching edges are consistent and counted onceWhen the next column is introduced, the options bucket is indexed by:the current occupied mask; andthe current outgoing matching mask  $R$ .Thus the incoming mask of the next column is exactly the outgoing mask of the preceding column. Both endpoints of each horizontal matching edge are checked to be  $P$ -vertices.The transition reward is
$$r(s,u)
=
\#T\text{ in the new column}
+\#\text{vertical matching edges in the new column}
+|R(s)|.$$
Each horizontal matching edge is therefore counted exactly once, when its right endpoint is introduced. Initialization counts only first-column  $T$ -vertices and vertical matching edges, since there are no incoming horizontal edges.A state with nonzero  $R$  describes a partial history with pending matching edges to the next column. Those edges are deliberately not yet charged. This convention is consistent in the seed vectors and in the subsequent potential calculation.Every occupied-neighbour condition at  $T$  is checkedFor a current  $T$ -vertex in row  $r$ , option_for computes
$$b(r)=
\mathbf 1_{\text{upper neighbour occupied}}
+\mathbf 1_{\text{lower neighbour occupied}}
+\mathbf 1_{\text{left neighbour occupied}}.$$
It rejects the option if  $b(r)>1$ , and records  $r$  in base_one when  $b(r)=1$ .When the next column is introduced, the conditionC++if (option.occupied & value.base_one) continue;forbids an occupied right neighbour opposite any already saturated  $T$ -vertex.This covers both possibilities exactly:If  $b(r)=1$ , the right neighbour must be unoccupied.If  $b(r)=0$ , either right-neighbour choice is permitted.All occupied neighbours count, whether labelled  $T$  or  $P$ . Every possible grid neighbour of a  $T$ -vertex is therefore accounted for before that vertex’s column is forgotten.Both boundaries are correctInitialization uses preceding occupancy  $o=0$  and incoming matching mask  $L=0$ , which gives the correct left boundary.At the right boundary, solve accepts only states with  $R=0$ . This prevents a matching endpoint from remaining unmatched through an outgoing stub. No further  $T$ -test is needed there: the missing right column contributes zero occupied neighbours, and the other neighbours have already been checked.Crucially, solve(4) and solve(5) return all reachable frontier states, including states with nonzero  $R$ . The final-boundary restriction is used to compute the reported closed-board maxima; it does not prune the state sets later used for the potential proof.The precise uniqueness statementThere is a bijection between:representative pairs  $(T,M)$  on the full board; andaccepted column histories with the correct left initialization and final condition  $R=0$ .Given a representative pair, its labels and horizontal matching masks are determined. Its remaining vertical matching is recovered uniquely by the path argument above, and its cumulative seam flags are determined.Conversely, an accepted history reconstructs a matching and a disjoint  $T$ , with all occupied-neighbour conditions satisfied.There is not a bijection between individual DP entries and representative pairs: many different histories can end in the same state. The code correctly retains only their maximum score. This loses no optimization information because the state determines all future feasibility conditions and rewards.Seam flags are handled correctlyThe horizontal seams between one-based rows  $2$ – $3$  and  $4$ – $5$  are crossed by vertical matching edges starting at zero-based rows  $1$  and  $3$ . Those are exactly the tests in vertical.The flags are accumulated by bitwise OR. They never prohibit a transition. Horizontal matching edges stay within one row and cannot cross these seams.Therefore all four possibilities—neither seam, either individual seam, and both seams—are represented without a hidden restriction.3. The potential verification proves the required universal inequalityThe stable set is closedLet  $S_4$  be the support returned by solve(4). The potential routine explicitly builds its state index from  $S_4$ .In every application of apply_one, it visits every state in that index and every legal outgoing option. Each resulting successor is looked up in the same index. Missing-successor detection occurs before the check involving the input potential value, so an outgoing edge cannot escape inspection merely because its value is negative infinity.The reproduced result
$$\texttt{missing\_transitions}=0$$
therefore proves
$$\operatorname{Succ}(S_4)\subseteq S_4.$$
This is the required closure under arbitrary subsequent columns.The run also gives
$$|S_4|=|S_5|=257{,}792,$$
and the odd-seed calculation successfully looks up every state of  $S_5$  in the  $S_4$  index. Hence  $S_5=S_4$ , as claimed.Equality is stronger than necessary: closure of  $S_4$  and inclusion of the odd seed in it already suffice for the parity argument.The max-plus operator has the correct directionThis is a decisive implementation detail. The source writes to output[i], indexed by the source state, using input[found->second], indexed by a successor. Thus its operator is
$$(\Phi f)(s)=\max_{s\to u}\bigl(r(s,u)+f(u)\bigr).$$
It follows that
$$(\Phi^2p)(s)
=
\max_{s\to u\to t}
\bigl(r(s,u)+r(u,t)+p(t)\bigr).$$
Therefore the entrywise inequality
$$\Phi^2p\le p+6$$
implies, for every legal two-column path  $s\to u\to t$ ,
$$r(s,u)+r(u,t)+p(t)\le6+p(s).$$
The verification loop is not restricted to edges attaining a forward DP maximum. It enumerates all legal successors from each stable state. The universal quantifier in the theorem is justified.The final inequality is checked independently of the search stopping ruleThe monotone iteration is a method for finding  $p$ . After it stops, the program applies the operator twice again and computes the maximum positive violation.Because largest_violation starts at zero, its reported value is technically
$$\max\left(0,\max_s\bigl(\Phi^2p(s)-6-p(s)\bigr)\right).$$
A reported zero therefore proves the desired nonpositive inequality.The fixed iteration limit is not a hidden mathematical assumption: the final inequality is checked separately. For this input, the iteration stabilizes after the reported four rounds anyway.The supplied table has one entry for each of the 257,792 states, with unique keys and integer potentials in  $\{0,1,2,3\}$ . Its minimum over final states  $R=0$  is zero. By exact seed maximization,
$$a_k\le V_k(s_k).$$
For even  $n=4+2q$ , sum the verified two-column inequalities:
$$a_n+p(s_n)
\le a_4+p(s_4)+6q
\le \max_s(V_4(s)+p(s))+6q
=12+6q.$$
The full board has  $R(s_n)=0$ , so the verified final minimum gives  $p(s_n)\ge0$ . Therefore
$$|T|+|M|=a_n\le12+6q=3n.$$
For odd  $n=5+2q$ , the same calculation yields
$$a_n+p(s_n)
\le16+6q,$$
hence
$$|T|+|M|\le16+6q=3n+1.$$
